Compiling one Java file with javac is easy. A real project has hundreds of files, dozens of libraries, tests, and a JAR to produce. A build tool does all of that with one command, the same way on every machine. In Java, that's almost always Maven or Gradle.

What a Build Tool Does

  • Downloads libraries (dependencies) and the libraries they need, from Maven Central.
  • Compiles your code and your tests.
  • Runs the tests, and stops the build if one fails.
  • Packages the result, usually as a JAR file.
  • Makes the build repeatable: a new teammate or the CI server runs the same command and gets the same result.

The Standard Layout

Both tools expect the same folders, so you rarely configure paths:

my-app/
├── pom.xml                (Maven)  or  build.gradle.kts (Gradle)
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/           your code: com/example/App.java
    │   └── resources/      config files, like application.properties
    └── test/
        └── java/           your tests: com/example/AppTest.java

Maven: pom.xml

Maven describes the project in an XML file, the POM (Project Object Model):

<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-app</artifactId>
  <version>1.0</version>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
      <version>6.1.3</version>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
  • groupId, artifactId and version identify your project, like a library's coordinates.
  • maven.compiler.release sets the Java version.
  • Each dependency is a library, found by its coordinates on Maven Central.

Maven Commands

Command Does
mvn compile Compiles the main code
mvn test Compiles and runs the tests
mvn package Tests, then builds the JAR in target/
mvn install Also copies the JAR to your local repository, for other projects
mvn clean Deletes target/, for a fresh build
mvn dependency:tree Shows every library and what brought it in

Commands run a lifecycle: mvn package also runs compile and test first. mvn clean package is the usual "build everything from scratch".

Gradle: build.gradle.kts

Gradle describes the build in code, usually Kotlin (build.gradle.kts), sometimes Groovy (build.gradle):

plugins {
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    implementation("com.google.guava:guava:33.4.5-jre")
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.12.1")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}

application {
    mainClass = "com.example.App"
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}

The java toolchain even downloads the right JDK version if it isn't installed. gradle init creates a project like this for you.

Gradle Commands

Command Does
./gradlew build Compiles, tests and packages (JAR in build/libs/)
./gradlew test Runs the tests
./gradlew run Runs the application
./gradlew clean Deletes build/
./gradlew dependencies Shows the dependency tree

Gradle only redoes what changed, and caches results, so repeat builds are fast.

Dependency Scopes

Not every library is needed everywhere:

Needed for… Maven scope Gradle configuration
Compiling and running the app compile (default) implementation
Tests only test testImplementation
Running, not compiling (drivers) runtime runtimeOnly
Compiling, provided by the server provided compileOnly

Putting JUnit in the test scope keeps it out of your production JAR.

The Wrapper: mvnw and gradlew

Projects usually include a wrapper script (./mvnw or ./gradlew) and commit it. It downloads the exact Maven or Gradle version the project needs, so nobody has to install anything, and everyone builds with the same version. Use the wrapper instead of a globally installed mvn or gradle.

Maven or Gradle?

Question Maven Gradle
Configuration XML, declarative, very uniform Kotlin or Groovy code, flexible
Learning curve Gentle Steeper for custom builds
Build speed Good Faster on big projects (caching)
Common in Enterprise and Spring projects Android, large multi-module builds

Both are excellent. Use whichever your team or project already uses. For a new Spring Boot app, either works; start.spring.io offers both.

The Answer in Short

  1. A build tool downloads libraries, compiles, tests and packages your project with one command.
  2. Both use the same layout: src/main/java for code, src/test/java for tests.
  3. Maven uses pom.xml and commands like mvn clean package; Gradle uses build.gradle.kts and ./gradlew build.
  4. Use scopes so test libraries stay out of the production JAR.
  5. Commit and use the wrapper, so everyone builds with the same version.
